name: Rose Pink
lede: Rose pink began as a cheap paint: red dye from brazilwood fixed onto chalk, sold to house painters and paper-stainers, and its odd name helped turn the word pink from a method into a color.

sections.title: Which rose pink
sections.body:
The swatch on this page, a hot, slightly purple pink, is the Wikipedia-list version of the name, and other sources disagree with it sharply [8]. Ridgway's 1912 plate XII gives a pale, cool pink about the same hue family but far lighter, and the crowd-sourced xkcd survey puts it at a warmer salmon-leaning pink [8]. ISCC-NBS 1955 files the name in block 38, and Maerz and Paul recorded it around 1850 [8]. Ridgway's first edition of 1886 already carried the name, which is the earliest dated source in our library [8]. Our nearest standard name for the screen swatch is [[hot-pink]], about 5 units away [8].

The pigment itself was not this bright. Dossie in 1764 calls it like red lake but made on a chalk base, and Field in 1835 calls it a coarse lake used for the commonest distempers [3]. Treat the swatch as a modern idea of rose pink, not a sample of the old paint.

sections.title: A word for a method
sections.body:
For a long time *pink* named a way of making a pigment, not a color. Ball explains that pinks were defined neither by their ingredients nor their color, and that the noun referred, like *lake*, to the method of synthesis: an organic colorant carried on an inorganic powder [1]. There were yellow pinks, made from weld, broom or unripe buckthorn berries, as well as green pinks, brown pinks and rose pinks [1][2][5].

Yellow pink was popular through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and Ball notes that it was often mixed with blue to give a green pink; Edward Norgate left a recipe for a pink in the seventeenth century [1]. The Compendium names French, Italian and Dutch pink as other yellow versions [2]. Rose pink was the one that was actually pink.

sections.title: Brazilwood on chalk
sections.body:
The earliest appearance of the English term that the Pigment Compendium can find is in the 1729 English edition of the *Traité de mignature*, usually attributed to Claude Boutet (1674), where the original French *lacque colombine* for a brazilwood lake was translated as rose pink [3]. In the seventeenth century the English name for it was *roset* [3]. Dossie (1764) says rose lake is commonly called rose pink, and that its dye came from [[flower:brazilwood|brazilwood]] or Campeachy wood, on a base that was usually chalk [3]. He adds that it was used mostly for house painting and wallpaper [3]. Field (1835) lists the dyewoods as Brazil, peach, sapan, bar and camwood, and says paper-stainers and the commonest distemper painters used it [3].

By the time of Heaton in 1928 the name was marked as obsolete or rare [3]. In use it also turned up in recipes, such as a Devonshire brown listed by Fishwick (1795 to 1816) that combined burnt umber, Frankfort black, rose pink and colcothar [4]. Brazilwood lakes are rarely identified in surviving paintings, which the Compendium blames on their evident lack of permanence [2]. A related name, [[brazil-red]], has its own article.

Books differ in detail here. Ball says rose pink made from brazilwood was considered different from the lake pigment made from the same colorant [1], while Dossie, as the Compendium quotes him, treats rose lake and rose pink as one thing [3].

sections.title: How pink became a color
sections.body:
Ball's account is that yellow pink fell out of use toward the end of the eighteenth century, and brown pink lingered into the nineteenth, until *pink* became synonymous with the light red rose pink and the meaning shifted from manufacture to color [1]. Paterson reaches the same view: rose pinks were probably instrumental in moving the word from the process to the color [5]. The Compendium dates the first use of the word for a light red to the middle of the seventeenth century, citing Harley, so the books disagree on the timing: mid-1600s in one, the late 1700s in another [3][1].

St Clair adds an observation [6]. Light reds got a name of their own while pale greens and yellows mostly did not, though some languages, Russian among them, distinguish more shades [6]. The article on [[pink]] picks up the story from there.

In the dictionary, rose pink today means a strong pink, a purplish pink or, most commonly, a light red-pink [5]. Its neighbors are [[carnation]], which Paterson glosses as rose-pink or flesh-colored [5], and [[rose-red]].

sections.title: Rose pink in the wild
sections.body: The name also turns up outside paint. Finlay describes the rose-pink [[gem:pearl|pearls]] of Scotland, exported across Europe for centuries, and a river pearler who said the sweet rose-pink pearls of the Oykel were always the most valuable [7]. In art, Ball notes that Yves Klein began with textured monochromes in golden yellows and deep rose pinks before he settled on a single color [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, none has a color within four units of this swatch covering even one per cent of the canvas [8]. That describes our archive, not painting as a whole, and fits a pigment that was a cheap, impermanent house paint [8][2]. Modern hot pink is far more saturated than any aged rose lake in a museum photograph [8].

The words are easier to follow than the paint. In Google Books, the phrase *rose pink* appears from around 1820, rises to a peak around 1950, and has since fallen to roughly a quarter of that level [8]. These counts include every use of the phrase, so they are not a clean measure of the color [8].

questions.q: What did the word pink originally name in painters' vocabulary?
choices: A way of making a pigment on a chalk-like base
A shade between red and white
questions.answer: A way of making a pigment on a chalk-like base

questions.q: True or false: every pink pigment was pink in color.

openers: Before pink was a color it was a method, and many pinks were yellow, green or brown.
Rose pink was a coarse chalk-and-brazilwood paint for houses and wallpaper, not a painter's refined lake.
